title: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
description: The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.John Ra
body: The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.John Ratcliffe reportedly arrived in the Russian capital earlier on Tuesday. Neither Washington or Moscow have confirmed the nature of the visit or who he was due to meet.In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday. It departed later on Tuesday.BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment. Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport.It departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appeared to have landed in the Russian capital at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from FlightRadar24. It returned to Riga shortly before 17:00 GMT.Footage on social media also purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow.Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.The trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, although he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow.John Foreman, who served as a British military attaché to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme that the visit could be focused on "escalation management" given speculation recent drone activity in Germany could be linked to Russia.He said: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."Foreman said the trip could also concern the release of US detainees currently being held in Russia.Ratcliffe played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina's, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine. The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, as well as former US marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term.Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.Additional reporting by Washington correspondent Daniel Bush and BBC Verify

schema.headline: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports

title: Trump says all mines cleared from Strait of Hormuz
description: US President Donald Trump has said that the US Navy has removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway which Iran has lar
body: US President Donald Trump has said that the US Navy has removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway which Iran has largely closed since the beginning of the war in the Middle East."Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.There is no comment from Iran. Closure of the strait has caused wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Trump has often said the US has control of the area - but Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission. Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the Strait of Hormuz before the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli air strikes against Iran.In addition to closing the strait, Iran retaliated against Israel and against US bases in the region as well as US Arab allies in the Gulf.A ceasefire aimed at facilitating talks to end the war has collapsed and there has been intermittent exchange of fire between the US and Iran. However, this week the US announced a raft of economic sanctions against Iran.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June - a 14-point document which set a 60-day deadline to reach a deal on the Strait of Hormuz, before substantial negotiations on resolving the nuclear issue - allegations that Iran is building a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has consistently denied.However, that deadline has now expired and talks have collapsed leading to the new US sanctions that Trump believes will lead to the collapse of the Iranian regime.Iran has been under sanctions for most of the time since the founding of the Islamic Republic in 1979 and Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he added would lead to "another defeat" for the US.Its economy, however, has suffered as a result of the war - and a blockade of Iranian ports that the US has been maintaining for weeks not to allow trade to continue. On Tuesday, China - the biggest buyer of Iranian oil - said it was firmly opposed to what it called the US's "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights. The US announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.Iran, for its part, has indicated that it wants to establish full control of the Strait of Hormuz - a view that is opposed by the US and most other countries which believe that the passage constitutes international waters and transit should remain unimpeded as it was before the war.Until recently - and on the basis of the MoU - Iran had been involved in negotiations with Oman, a US ally, to agree a mechanism for administering the strait. However, those talks have so far not produced an agreement and, last week, Trump even threatened to bomb its ally "if it gets in the way" of his administration's own talks with Iran over the issue.Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Tuesday that he hoped his country and Iran would soon announce the establishment of a temporary shipping corridor in the strait after meeting his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran.He said in a statement he also hoped for "practical arrangements" to restore safe navigation, adding: "Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course."

schema.headline: Trump says all mines cleared from Strait of Hormuz

title: Spanish government says sorry to people of Ceuta for migrant crisis
description: The Spanish government has apologised to the people of Ceuta for the migrant crisis that has affected the city for weeks and it has unveiled plans to
body: The Spanish government has apologised to the people of Ceuta for the migrant crisis that has affected the city for weeks and it has unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws."I want to apologise to all those who may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared for," Defence Minister Margarita Robles told a parliamentary committee."I have witnessed first-hand your feelings of anxiety, of abandonment, of lack of safety."At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa on 30 and 31 July. Most of the migrants swam around the border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas.The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most sleeping rough on beaches or streets.The Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has been under mounting pressure to resolve the situation, with many residents and the local authorities in Ceuta, which has a population of 84,000, complaining that it is unsustainable.The Sánchez government has now declared a situation of interest for national security in the city, centralising management of the crisis. Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres has been tasked with co-ordinating the response, relieving the Ceuta local government of that responsibility.Coinciding with the government's moves and Robles's parliamentary appearance – the first by ministers on this issue over the coming days – changes were also announced to migration and asylum legislation.Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said the reforms would seek to ensure Spain that was fully in line with new EU regulations and that its process was "orderly, efficient, and... [provided] all possible guarantees". It will include limiting to three days the amount of time an undocumented migrant can spend undergoing medical, biometric and legal evaluation on arrival – EU regulations allow this period to last up to seven days.The reforms will also create a two-speed system for processing asylum requests, in theory accelerating cases deemed urgent.However, the information provided by government ministers has left some questions unanswered. Robles told parliament that agents of the CNI intelligence service had shared information about a possible imminent migrant crossing with security forces shortly before it happened, but Grande-Marlaska appeared to contradict her."There was no report that hinted that on 30 July what eventually happened was going to happen," he said. Robles later said that the information had not been conveyed via a report.Sánchez has blamed traffickers and social media activity for the mass crossing. However, many others have pointed the finger at Morocco, which in the past has been accused of using the borders with Ceuta and its sister city Melilla to pressure Madrid or the EU on political issues.

schema.headline: Spanish government says sorry to people of Ceuta for migrant crisis

title: Andrew Tate exaggerates and does not own supercars in photos, lawyers claim
description: Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated h
body: Controversial influencer Andrew Tate portrays himself as "uberwealthy" but did not own cars and a yacht featured on his social media and exaggerated his lifestyle for online attention, his legal representatives have said.Tate and his brother Tristan are currently being held in a Florida jail but are seeking release on bail while they await the outcome of extradition proceedings.They were arrested last month after British prosecutors unveiled new charges including alleged sexual offences against them, which both men deny. Prosecutors have argued the Tates are a "flight risk", citing the brothers' past statements about their wealth and influence and having multiple identities to evade the law.In a legal submission to the court, the brothers' legal representatives said the Tates' business model "depends on online attention". "The outrageousness of the posts by them and about them is the point. The more hyperbolic and outlandish the post, the more likely it will generate views and likes, which in turn generates income. In short, they are playing a role," it says.At times Andrew Tate has also exaggerated and used hyperbole for "comedic effect" with no intention to be taken seriously, the submission argues. "The government alleges that the Tates are a risk of flight based on their social media claims that they are 'self-proclaimed billionaires' who own 'high-end vehicles, private jets, and a custom $50-million-dollar superyacht and have unrestricted access to traditional funds, cryptocurrency, and bitcoin,'" it says. "But the government has not established these grandiose claims are true," it adds.

schema.headline: Andrew Tate exaggerates and does not own supercars in photos, lawyers claim

title: Dolly Parton obituary: The country legend who sang from the heart
description: Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millionsFigure caption, Dolly Parton: The life of a legendary country singerByTiffany Werth
body: Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millionsFigure caption, Dolly Parton: The life of a legendary country singerByTiffany Wertheimer and Emma PetrieDolly Parton, the country singer from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, will be remembered for her songs that told beautiful stories so honestly, such as Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You.In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy.”She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her showbusiness career that spanned more than 60 years.Image source, Getty Images/Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Dolly Parton aged nineDolly Rebecca Parton was born in 1946, the fourth of 12 children, into a poor farming family who lived in a one-bedroom cabin in Tennessee.   Her father, Robert Lee Parton, was a tobacco farmer and paid a missionary a sack of cornmeal for delivering her.There was already music in the family - her mother, Avie Lee, sang folk songs all the time and her aunt played the guitar and wrote songs. During some of Parton's earliest performances, her uncle, Bill Owens, accompanied her on the guitar - formative years for the future music legend.From the age of six, she sang in the local church where her grandfather was the pastor, and was performing on her local TV station by the time she was a teenager.In 1959, when she was 13 years old, Parton performed with Uncle Bill at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville - a live broadcast that is regarded as country music's biggest stage.She was introduced by Johnny Cash and received three encores.Image source, Getty Images//Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Nineteen-year-old Dolly Parton in Nashville, 1965The 'town tramp'During her teenage years, Parton began to model herself on a local character who was known as the “town tramp”.  The lady wore bright red nail polish, low-cut tops and high heels - young Dolly thought she was beautiful.  When people said to her: “She ain’t nothing but trash”, Parton would reply: "Well, that’s what I’m gonna be when I grow up”.Parton sang “I’m just a backwards Barbie / too much make-up, too much hair”, but her image was both a coat of armour and an astute disguise that helped get her noticed in showbusiness. She would get ahead of the jokes by making them first, and had a quick and simple response for anyone who suggested she should tone it down: "Go to hell."Image source, Getty Images/CBS photo ArchiveImage caption, Parton said she felt better in bright colours and shiny clothes on stage: "You'd be surprised how much it costs to look this cheap"After graduating from high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville to launch her singing career and met her future husband, Carl Dean, on her very first day.They married two years later and remained together until his death in 2025.In Nashville, Parton's singing caught the eye of country performer Porter Wagoner, who hired her to perform on his television programme.Over the next seven years, the pair became one of country music's most popular duos, releasing so many duets that many fans assumed they were a couple.But their relationship was a complicated one, and as Parton's solo career started to rise, so did tensions behind the scenes.Writing in her book Star of the Show: My Life on Stage, Parton said Wagoner saw her success away from his show as a "threat".Image source, Getty Images/Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Dolly Parton with Porter Wagoner on the set of his TV show in 1967While travelling with Wagoner on a tour bus in 1969, Parton wrote Coat of Many Colors, a beautifully emotive tale of how she grew up poor, but rich with love. Scrawled on the back of one of Wagoner's dry cleaning receipts, it was rated by Rolling Stone magazine, external as her second best-ever song. Years later, Parton named her own children's book Coat of Many Colors, and it was the name of a 2015 TV movie based on her life."It's a song that's just stood by me... it's created a life of many colours for me," she said.Image source, Getty Images/Ethan MillerImage caption, Dolly Parton won several awards for her made-for-TV movie Coat of Many Colors'Sad little country song'Despite being unable to read sheet music, Parton played several instruments including the banjo, harp, piano and saxophone.She had her first number one hit - and first Grammy nomination - with the song Joshua in 1971 and finally left The Porter Wagoner Show in 1974 to concentrate on her solo career.To say goodbye to him, she wrote I Will Always Love You, a song that many think is about two lovers parting ways."That's the prettiest song I ever heard," Wagoner cried when he first heard it, her website says.The same year, Elvis Presley was set to record a cover of the song, but Parton pulled the deal when his manager demanded half of the songwriting rights.She cried all night at the difficult decision, and Priscilla Presley later told her that Elvis sang the song to her during their divorce.In 1992, Whitney Houston transformed it into a now-iconic power ballad. Parton said she was driving when she first heard the cover and had to pull over: “When I heard her go from the a cappella into the music part, I honestly thought I was going to have a heart attack, it was one of the most overwhelming things.”Houston's cover of Parton's “sad little country song” was one of the proudest moments of her life, she said.Parton re-recorded the song for The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, a 1982 film in which she starred and was nominated for a Golden Globe for best actress.That other womanAnother of her most famous songs was released in 1974 - Jolene.Showing her aching vulnerability, it's about a bank clerk with flaming locks of auburn hair who flirted with her husband."Jolene, I'm begging of you, please don't take my man," she pleads.Parton said her husband, who was notoriously private, was a bit embarrassed by the song. But it was nothing serious - just a running joke between them: "I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"The song has been covered by many artists including The White Stripes, Miley Cyrus and Beyoncé, who changed up to the lyrics to the more ominous: "I'm warning you, don't come for my man." In the years to come, Dolly Parton's success only grew, with more hits, nominations and awards - she won her first Grammy in 1978 for Here You Come Again. Image source, Richard McCaffrey/Michael Ochs ArchiveImage caption, "If you see someone without a smile, give 'em one of yours": Parton performing in California in 1978Playing her acrylic nailsIt was the theme song that Dolly Parton wrote for the 1980 movie 9 to 5 that fully propelled her to stardom.Actress Jane Fonda, who produced and starred in the film about women being discriminated against in the workplace, made a deal with Parton - she'd star in the film if she could also write the theme song.Realising her nails clicking together sounded like a typewriter, she wrote 9 to 5 while waiting around on set. Fonda said she realised straight away that it wasn't just a theme song - it was an anthem.The film was a big success at the box office and the song won several awards, including a Golden Globe.Image source, Getty Images/Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Dolly Parton in a scene from 9 to 5'I look like a woman but I think like a man'Parton was a successful and shrewd businesswoman, and in 2022 was listed by Forbes as one of America's richest self-made women, external."I look like a woman but I think like a man. I've done business with men who think I'm as silly as I look. By the time they realise I'm not, I've got the money and gone," she once said.Her physical appearance - the costumes, wigs, long painted nails and high heels - were merely a facade of a stereotypical “dumb blonde”. But she always said she knew she wasn't dumb "and I also know that I'm not blonde".She had her own record label, Dolly Records, and co-owned The Dollywood Company, which manages entertainment venues, a theme park, a water park and a resort.In 1986, she opened her Dollywood amusement park in the foothills of her beloved Smoky Mountains. As well as rollercoasters, it is home to the largest sanctuary for non-releasable bald eagles in the world. Its rehabilitation and breeding work has won awards and in 2007, the bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list.Image source, Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty ImagesImage caption, Parton, pictured at Dollywood in 1993, said she wanted to build a place where the culture of the Smoky Mountains could be celebratedDespite her wealth and success, Parton remained humble and supported the communities where she grew up.Inspired by her father who couldn’t read or write, she launched the Imagination Library in 1999, which gave free books to children in Tennessee. It has since expanded to Australia, the UK, Ireland and Canada, sending out millions of free books every year.Her non-profit organisation, The Dollywood Foundation, has funded scholarships, hospitals and donated to flood and wildfire victims.In 2020, as the Covid-19 pandemic griped the world, Parton donated $1m (£716,000) to the Vanderbilt University Medical Centre which helped to fund the Moderna vaccine. In later years, Parton had to postpone or cancel several shows for health treatment.In May 2026, she postponed an upcoming Las Vegas residency because of treatment for kidney stones, saying it would take some time to heal and be "stage-performance ready"."I can't be dizzy carrying around banjos, guitars and such on five-inch heels - and you know that I'm going to be wearing them," she said in a video message. "Not to mention all those heavy rhinestone outfits, the big hair, my big... uh, personality," she joked.Image source, Brandon Sloter/Image Of Sport/Getty ImagesImage caption, Parton amazed fans when she performed at the NFL Thanksgiving half-time show in 2023, aged 77Parton spoke graciously throughout her career with humour and intelligence. She steered clear of politics, saying she didn't want to alienate half her audience. She was a courageous and talented trailblazer for country music at a time when women were not taken seriously in the industry, especially as solo artists.Parton said she hoped to be remembered for her songwriting and as somebody who took her work seriously, but not herself.She once offered this advice: “Never ignore your roots, your home, or your hair."It's guidance that she stayed true to throughout her life.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton obituary: The country legend who sang from the heart

title: Man dies in crash after Stratford-upon-Avon police pursuit
description: A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmi
body: A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics. The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said. Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.It later reopened. "We made a mandatory referral to the IOPC because a death had occurred following police contact. "They have declared an independent investigation and we will co-operate fully with their investigation."The IOPC said the investigation was at an early stage and confirmed its officials attended the police's post-incident operation to gather information. "We understand the driver of a black Audi A3 failed to stop for police and was then pursued for around six minutes before the vehicle was involved in a collision with a car being driven by a member of the public," a spokesperson said."We are also appealing for any car footage of the pursuit that other motorists may have recorded. Our investigators can be contacted at 0300 303 5609 or by email: WarwickRoadPursuit@policeconduct.gov.uk"We have met with the families of the driver and the seriously injured woman to explain our role and will keep them regularly updated throughout our investigation, which is at an early stage."Manuela Perteghella, Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-on-Avon, said the incdent was "incredibly tragic". "My thoughts are with the families of all those impacted. We must now let the investigation take its course."Works were carried out on Warwick Road two years ago, aimed at reducing the number of crashes in the area.Warwickshire County Council added a one-way system, lowered the speed limit and implemented a protected turning lane at the Ingon Lane junction.Street lighting was also boosted to improve visibility for crossing pedestrians at Fisherman's Car Park.

schema.headline: Man dies in crash after Stratford-upon-Avon police pursuit

title: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?
description: China is the biggest buyer of Iranian goods, making up 26.9% of its exports in 2025, according data from the International Trade Centre (ITC), a subsi
body: China is the biggest buyer of Iranian goods, making up 26.9% of its exports in 2025, according data from the International Trade Centre (ITC), a subsidiary of the United Nations and the World Trade Organisation.There a few caveats to ITC's data, which covers a period before the US-Israel war with Iran began.First, several economists believe that even before the conflict started, a lot of Iranian oil sales, particularly to China, were underreported for political reasons.Second, the ITC tallies Iran's exports using mostly the import numbers reported by its trading partners - owing to the difficulty in getting up to date export data from Iran.Third, import data for some of Iran's trading partners, such as Iraq, is incomplete.Despite this, Iranian trade's importance to China is clear from its response to the US announcement of "economic D-Day".It said that it was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions", that economic pressure tactics would not help resolve problems and that Beijing would safeguard its own interests.Like Turkey, Pakistan borders Iran and is one of its biggest export partners, according to ITC data, while also being keen to maintain a good relationship with the US.But unlike Turkey, Pakistan's top export partner is instead the US, meaning it has more to lose from any economic punishment imposed by Washington.It is also a key mediator in peace talks between the US and Iran, meaning a breakdown in its relationship with either country could make finding a solution to the conflict even more challenging.The other complicating factor is that not all of Pakistan's trade with Iran is within the Pakistan government's control.The BBC has seen evidence that oil is being smuggled across the border from Iran to Pakistan en masse by bikers, some as young as 15.This was the case before the Iran war began, but data suggests the practice has picked up since.And though the US and Pakistan's oil firms have pressured Pakistan's government to clamp down on the practice, it has struggled to police remote parts of the 900km border.The BBC has previously asked the Iranian government to comment on the allegation that it is involved in the fuel smuggling. It did not respond.US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the sanctions against Iran will "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue".Yet, many experts disagree. Advisory firm Oxford Economics said the direct impact on Iran's revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".Ali Vaez, deputy director at the International Crisis Group, said: "Anything that moves in Iran has already been sanctioned by multiple layers of sanctions, in fact. "So the question now is one of enforcement. Does the United States have what it takes to impose fines and levies on countries that continue to trade with Iran?"He noted how the US started an economic war with China, Iran's biggest trading partner, last year but "backed out of it".Former senior advisor at the state department Aya Ibrahim said the US's overreliance on them "incentivises countries to find ways around that system".She also raised concerns that the sanctions may have the biggest affect on people, rather than economies, as they "deny people necessities to stay alive".Meanwhile, global markets have had a muted response to the announcement.Global oil prices fell following the announcement, but are still far higher than pre-war levels. Stock traders were even less moved by the news, with the major indexes of the biggest companies listed in the US, Europe, and Asia barely shifting.The US will has a way to go before it convinces economists, investors, and the nations trading with Iran that its sanctions threat is to be taken seriously.Additional reporting by Miguel Roca-Terry

schema.headline: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?

title: Father's house was rammed by car before son died in A66 crash
description: A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.Cole Worthy, 17, was
body: A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.Meanwhile, nine men and three women, aged between 18 and 61, were arrested across Teesside on Monday as part of the investigation into the lead-up to the crash. They were held on a range of offences, including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.Two men have since been charged.Kai Beattie, of Foxrush Court, Redcar, has been charged with possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.Cameron George, of Micklow Close, Redcar, has been charged with possession of class A and class B drugs with intent to supply, and possession of criminal property.Cleveland Police said on Tuesday that five further arrests had been made, including a 16-year-old boy and two men, 18 and 21, who were held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group. A 55-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and a 23-year-old man on suspicion of making threats to kill.All five remain in custody.

schema.headline: Father's house was rammed by car before son died in A66 crash

title: Why some US restaurants are banning tips
description: 'What you see is what you pay' - why some US restaurants are banning tipsImage source, Caroline KraetzerImage caption, Caroline Kraetzer no longer get
body: 'What you see is what you pay' - why some US restaurants are banning tipsImage source, Caroline KraetzerImage caption, Caroline Kraetzer no longer gets tips but her salary is double the normBySuzanne Bearne Wine waiter Caroline Kraetzer earns $40 (£30) an hour, double what most service staff in San Francisco are paid but then it costs a lot to eat at her restaurant.At a set price of $140 (£100) per person, La Cigale is one of a small number of US restaurants charging higher prices so it can pay high salaries - and it doesn't allow tips.It tells customers: "What you see is what you pay. We do not accept tips, your kind words and return visits will suffice."Kraetzer says it is good to no longer be "reliant on the generosity of strangers to pay the bills".While waiting staff at other restaurants can make a lot of money from tips, she says "you're often there two hours before service, and again when you're closing after the guests have left, so you are making minimum wage during that time".Fairer for staff?On the other side of the US, Rachel Miller, chef and owner of Nightshade Noodle Bar in the town Lynn, Massachusetts, moved to a tip-free model five years ago when they reopened after the Covid-19 pandemic.Her motivation was to make it fairer for the kitchen staff. "The people breaking their backs and minds in the kitchen - often the least visible and the least celebrated - were taking home a fraction of what the front staff made on tips for the same hours," she says.Miller says she found it "deeply unsettling" to see higher tips going to white male staff and lower tips to everyone else. "Tipping lets guests, consciously or not, pay people differently based on gender, race, or sexuality and I was not willing to let that decide my team's income."To pay the staff higher wages, Miller also increased prices at the French-Vietnamese restaurant. Its tasting menus now start from $102 (£75) for seven courses before 18:00, and $126 (£92) for nine courses."Our prices are higher than a comparable restaurant's because they carry the full cost of paying people properly," says Miller. "That is the trade, and I stand behind it."Image source, Alyssa BlumsteinImage caption, Rachel Miller says that banning tips is fairer for her kitchen staffTip-free can mean higher pricesYet not every restaurant that has switched to a tipless model has made a success of it, as sometimes customers don't appreciate the higher menu prices.Talulla in Cambridge, Massachusetts, dropped tips in 2020 so it could pay staff more equitably, only to then switch back in September of last year."We tried to keep our non-tipping model simply by raising our menu prices 23%, but we were only able to sustain this through the winter months," says co-owner Danielle Ayer."Operating a non-tipped restaurant is more expensive overall," adds Ayer. This is because tips don't count as part of a restaurant's revenues, but higher menu prices do. So if a venue increases prices to pay staff more, its revenues go up accordingly, and it must pay more sales tax.William Michael Lynn, professor of food and beverage management at Cornell University and author of The Psychology of Tipping, says the problem of going tip-free is that customers struggle to get their heads around the maths."Higher menu prices make dining out seem more expensive because people do not adequately take into account that they are no longer tipping," he says. "It leads to lower demand."Image source, Amanda CohenImage caption, Amanda Cohen says customers are pleased when they realise they don't have to tipIn New York, vegetarian restaurant Dirt Candy was one of the very first to ban tipping back in 2015. "I wanted to make it more equal for everybody," says chef and owner Amanda Cohen, who now pays her staff about $30 an hour.She says that many customers "are pleasantly surprised when they realise they don't have to tip 20% on top".Cassidy Van der Kamp is a filmmaker whose YouTube documentary Tipless was inspired by her own experience of working in a restaurant in Oakland, California which went tip-free.While some other servers left, Van der Kamp, who was originally paid about $10 an hour plus tips, decided to stay and earned $21 per hour after the change."I had stability for the first time as I knew what I was earning… and I didn't need to look at a low tip and think what did I do wrong?"'Tipping fatigue'While Van der Kamp liked the move, Lynn says that a huge challenge of moving to a gratuity-free system is that it can be difficult to attract and retain waiting staff who like getting tips.However, given the growth of what has been called "tipping fatigue" – people being increasingly annoyed at having to pay high tips – will more restaurants stop the practice?"Despite tip-fatigue, I do not think tipping is going to be eliminated on widescale anytime soon because the economic disadvantages of eliminating tipping outweigh the advantages," says Lynn.Back at Nightshade Noodle Bar, Miller doesn't regret her decision. "The clearest measure is that staff stay."Turnover in this industry is brutal, and we have people who have been here since we made the change. It has proven to be highly valued by my guests and team."

schema.headline: Why some US restaurants are banning tips

title: Boy, 3, attacked by crocodile in Huntingdon recovers at home
description: The fundraising page was set up to support the family financially and help the boy's recovery and rehabilitation.It has raised more than £113,000 to d
body: The fundraising page was set up to support the family financially and help the boy's recovery and rehabilitation.It has raised more than £113,000 to date.His parents said the money donated so far had supported them "financially to cover immediate costs such as our bills and mortgage", and to "cover our loss of wages during this time".They said they had been able to buy new toys for the paediatric intensive care unit at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge and donate money to the Sick Children's Trust charity.They said they also want to donate to the Addenbrooke's Charitable Trust (ACT) to thank staff who were involved in their son's care "including the supply of superhero costumes to brighten up his day".They thanked everyone who had "shown such kindness and generosity during what has been a considerable ordeal for us all".The BBC understands the arrested man, who did not know the child, has learning disabilities and was on a trip with carers.He was released on bail until 18 September and police said he was "assessed as not being fit for interview".Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? title: Food influencers v critics: Why credibility counts
description: Image source, Oscar BostockImage caption, "Creators certainly have an influence on how people go out to eat, for sure," says Bristol influencer Oscar
body: Image source, Oscar BostockImage caption, "Creators certainly have an influence on how people go out to eat, for sure," says Bristol influencer Oscar BostockByJasmine Ketibuah-FoleyWest of EnglandWhen stuck for ideas about where to eat on a Friday night or torn between takeaways, more and more people are turning to social media and their favourite content creators for inspiration.Research by one Bristol food writer has raised questions about transparency, with some creators guaranteeing positive coverage in advance and offering not to make clear their review was in exchange for a free meal.Those promises of good reviews were made before they had eaten a bite - or realised the restaurant they had been asked to promote did not exist.So can diners trust influencers to give an honest opinion and what is their role in shaping where we eat? We asked people in the food scene to share their thoughts.Meg Houghton-Gilmour, food writer and founder of The Bristol Sauce, undertook a two-part research piece, external into the world of food influencing when she created a website and social media account for a fake Japanese restaurant "coming soon to Bristol". She messaged 48 influencers asking how much they would charge to make content, what would guarantee positive coverage and whether they would declare it an advert.After receiving 33 responses, she said the prices quoted by influencers varied widely. Some said they would post in exchange for free food and drink, without an extra payment on top - and five of those said they would post without labelling the content as an advert.UK advertising rules state paid posts must be clearly marked with #ad or a platform's paid partnership feature. This includes free meals in exchange for posts.Houghton-Gilmour added the requests she sent out had created a swell of "misleading" positive noise on social media around the upcoming opening."I realised how insular and repetitive it is. Everyone going to the same places, saying the same thing," she said.Image source, Meg Houghton-GilmourImage caption, Meg Houghton-Gilmour said her research offered "a fascinating insight" into the world of influencersWith more than 135,000 followers on Instagram, external and millions of views on TikTok, external, Oscar Bostock, also known as Bos Finesse, is a driving force as a food creator in Bristol and said becoming an influencer was a "no-brainer"."There are food creators in the social media space, like myself, who do have a lot of credibility. But we need to respect the culture a bit as well."You'll never beat the people that write about food for a living. I don't really like to review and criticise food - I'll leave that to the professionals. "At the same time, you need people here like myself to just celebrate food," he adds.Bostock says authenticity is very important to him, and told the BBC there are many places he has said no to reviewing or reflecting. "It's worth explaining it, being paid for a restaurant to say, 'this is good' is completely different to being  paid to promote a new menu or venue. "I feel very strongly about it, anywhere I work with had to be a place I actually valued and would visit in my own time."Image source, Jay RaynerImage caption, Consumers needed to know whether someone had paid for the meal they were talking about, said food critic Jay RaynerFood critic Jay Rayner, who writes for the Financial Times, believes his role is to write "as interesting, entertaining [and] truthful column" as he can."I don't think there's much truth in the idea that the newspaper critic is dead," he said. "What I see happening is an awful lot more media around restaurants, full stop."I know, anecdotally, that a good review from me still results in many bookings, which is lovely - but it's not actually a concern of mine."He said people sometimes ask if influencers "pose a challenge to what you do"."My response is, 'only if it's better than what I do'," said Rayner, stressing his authority as a critic is not unassailable. "I do not have a right to my lofty perch."Rayner said newspapers such as the Financial Times would "pick up the bill" for critics writing reviews, whereas a lot of influencers were invited to eat for nothing, which is something consumers should be aware of."That does undermine the credibility of the review," he said. "[But] you know, we're all celebrating the culture of eating food and eating out."Image source, Adam ArmstrongImage caption, Chef Adam Armstrong said influencers, like critics, offer an opinion which "you don't have to look at"Adam Armstrong, head chef at Bath's Emberwood, said the sort of promotion restaurants received from influencers was something the industry would have been "screaming out for" years ago."If you make a bit of noise here or there, it just puts you on the map," he said.He acknowledged many people had a "negative" view of food creators, but added: "People give them too much reverence in the first place. They're just people with an opinion."The Nook Cheltenham, in Gloucestershire, has worked hard at being Instagram-friendly, currently boasting more than 11,000 followers.Director and founder Edward Surman said: "Social media is a place where brands can alter their own story - where it's not moved around by the press."Surman maintains influencers are not replacing food critics, but more of an "augmentation". Image source, Baljinder Kaur Sangha-GillImage caption, Baljinder Kaur Gill said influencers had opened up the conversation about foodWiltshire-based food influencer Baljinder Kaur Sangha-Gill, also known as The Authentic Punjabee, says her pages have moved beyond a list of recommendations and have come to represent a community of friends."Influencers haven't replaced critics. We've just opened the conversation about food," she said."Years ago, when you were looking for a restaurant or recipe, you'd wait for the Sunday paper. Now you can just go onto TikTok."But she cautions not everything on social media is reliable."People will get free things to promote something. You've got to be aware of that. I'm very careful with that, I don't lie to my followers," she added.Following her research, Houghton-Gilmour added: "Influencers are a symptom of the society and tech world we live in - not the problem. It's the tech billionaires making it unclear what's an ad and what's not."She said the problem was not people making content but the lack of transparency, although she accepted that was not true of all influencers.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Bristol

schema.headline: Food influencers v critics: Why credibility counts

title: Brydon Carse: Joe Root says he is 'hacked off' and 'disappointed' at nightclub incident
description: England captain Joe Root says he is "hacked off" and "disappointed" at the incident involving fast bowler Brydon Carse at a Derby nightclub.Carse, 31,
body: England captain Joe Root says he is "hacked off" and "disappointed" at the incident involving fast bowler Brydon Carse at a Derby nightclub.Carse, 31, was dropped from the squad for the second Test starting against Pakistan this week. Images that appeared on social media on Sunday showed Carse in handcuffs outside a bar in Derby on Saturday night and he was briefly arrested and subsequently de-arrested."If I'm being brutally honest, I'm really hacked off, I'm really disappointed," Root said in the opening to a news conference."After last week's performance, we're sat here and we're talking about something that is not related to it at all."The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has referred the incident to the Cricket Regulator and Carse was replaced in the squad by Sonny Baker, with the Test starting at Lord's on Thursday.Carse was not on England duty at the time of the incident as he was released to play for Durham, but he is a centrally contracted player. Root also said he had spoken to his England team-mate about the incident, and expressed his frustration at the "stupid mistakes" that are continually being made."I've spoken to Brydon, and when I first found out my main concern was him as a person," Root added."I don't think I'm speaking out of turn by saying he's very upset, very apologetic and understands his actions. I'm sure that when he gets his chance he will say that himself. "But I don't think it's the isolated incident itself, it's the fact we keep making stupid mistakes away from the game and it's detracting from what we're doing on the field."In October, England white-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer outside a nightclub in Wellington, New Zealand, with team-mates Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue also present.During the Ashes tour of Australia, opener Ben Duckett was filmed apparently drunk on England's holiday in Noosa.And in June, former Test captain Ben Stokes and pace bowler Gus Atkinson broke a team curfew and were present when a member of England's security staff was punched by a Saracens rugby player in a London nightclub.In this latest incident, Carse was with Durham team-mates Stokes and Matthew Potts, all of whom are under England central contracts. In Stokes' case, the England deal remains in place despite his international retirement in June.It makes a total of eight contracted players who have been involved in or present for late-night incidents in the past year – more than a quarter of the 30 men on England deals.When he was reappointed as Test captain, Root confirmed he would remove the midnight curfew which was previously in place during Stokes and Brendon McCullum's regime after a string of off-field incidents during the Ashes over the winter.Root stood by that decision, saying he still did not think it was "the right way to go", but admitted it would take some time for the team to be trusted by the fans again. "In many ways we're going to have to earn a lot of trust back, and it's something that we're going to have to live and breathe consistently," he said."I might only be in this dressing room for a couple more years, but there is a group of players there who might be in there for another 10. "We've had a very strong discussion about what's expected of everyone when they play for England, what the standards are that we have to uphold, not just on the field but off it."I've made it very clear how we want to conduct ourselves, and now we've got to live it and show people what I see day in, day out in the dressing room, which is a group of characters who know what it means to play for England and not having incidents define how we are seen as players. That's going to take some work and time."Root also confirmed he had spoken to his predecessor Stokes, who was also seen in the social media video, but only to check in on Carse's wellbeing.He was asked what potential consequences Carse might face but said he would have no involvement as it is in the hands of the regulator, and was keen to reiterate that he was focusing on moving forward and "building something to be proud of"."I don't think the recent past has been a good look," Root, 35, said."It's our responsibility to change that. I see the dressing room every day and how we operate around cricket and it's very impressive. "But at the same time, I can understand why we are viewed in a certain way and in a certain light at the moment. "That's what lies ahead of us, to change that. I just think, if we don't put ourselves in certain situations, it's not something we will have to worry about."If there was any question as to why England turned to Joe Root for a second stint as Test captain, if he is the right man for the job, then this address at Lord's removed all of those doubts.Root showed himself to be the leader England need in this moment. Clearly ticking over what happened at the weekend, Root was able to strike the balance between letting his feelings be known, showing compassion for Brydon Carse and not pre-judging the investigation that is ongoing.There have been plenty of these kinds of news conferences over the past year: someone wearing an England badge explaining a misdemeanour, promising to do better. This time, when Root spoke, his words were plausible and believable.Some wondered why Root was the one left to face the media, rather than members of the management team like director of cricket Rob Key or chief executive Richard Gould.Maybe it is because no-one else was able to speak with Root's gravitas. No-one in a suit, not Ben Stokes, nor Harry Brook. Perhaps this is the most impressive display of leadership anyone connected with English cricket has shown for some time.It should leave no one – especially not the England players – in any doubt where their captain stands on this issue. For any athlete to tell the world they are "hacked off" with a team-mate is a stark message.Root addressed his England team on Tuesday morning. If the captain was able to speak like this in public, one can only wonder about the sternness of the message delivered in private. Carse would not have been there, but plenty of others who have erred in the past year would have been in the room.There will be no return for the midnight curfew, but Root was also quite clear about players avoiding situations that could lead to trouble. "Stupid mistakes", he called them. He hammered home the point that players will not find trouble if they do not put themselves in the places where trouble could find them.But Root also regularly mentioned the notion of this team now having an opportunity to build something on and off the field. Put simply, their reputation in the eyes of the public cannot get much lower, so the only direction is improvement.Amid all the controversy, English cricket is fortunate to have Root. Not only is he a bona fide all-time great, but also a superb example of how all sportspeople should go about their business on and off the field.Last week, before his first Test back in charge, Root asked his players to be "good role models and good human beings". They should look no further than their captain for inspiration.

schema.headline: Brydon Carse: Joe Root says he is 'hacked off' and 'disappointed' at nightclub incident

title: Sir Billy Boston: 'A world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told'
description: When Sir Billy Boston was knighted in 2025, it was a unique moment for rugby league.For the first time, this rebel sport from the north of England had
body: When Sir Billy Boston was knighted in 2025, it was a unique moment for rugby league.For the first time, this rebel sport from the north of England had been recognised in such a manner; one of its heroes had been acknowledged for their contribution to history through the game.Sir Billy was a fitting recipient of the honour and a world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told.You can tell the importance of someone by how many statutes have been erected in tribute, and Sir Billy Boston wasn't lacking.His name was chosen as one of just five to grace Wembley's monument to rugby league's Challenge Cup, while years after his departure north, his home city of Cardiff also ensured his legacy remained cast-iron strong as he formed part of a three-man tribute along with Clive Sullivan and Gus Risman.Unsurprisingly, Boston is also captured in bronze in his adopted home of Wigan; the place where his legend really came to life.Born and brought up in Cardiff's ethnically-eclectic Tiger Bay district, he learned his rugby skills on the streets and with the talent factory-esque Cardiff International Athletic Club. Like all Welsh lads he harboured dreams of playing for his local club Cardiff RFC and hopefully the national team.Like others before and after for a time, Boston found those routes blocked, having to travel to Neath and Pontypridd to trial before his military service took him north.It was here where the league scouts came calling, and Wigan persuaded Boston to turn professional in 1953, forever ending his union dreams in the time of 'sine die' penalties for liaising with league personnel.The money was life changing. £3,000 could easily buy a house at that stage, while it proved money well spent as he took to the new code like a duck to water, scoring with his first touch in a Wigan A team game.This prime specimen of Welsh breezeblock had everything; he was quick, he could step and as former player and BBC commentator Ray French put it - his fend was like "being hit in the face with shovel".The sepia footage and slow shutter speeds of the cameras that captured his magic during his playing days simply cannot dull his brilliance. Whether it was bustling over for another try in cherry and white hoops at Wembley or crushing the Aussies at Sydney Cricket Ground, Boston was a blur of speed, footwork and power.Having swiftly progressed to the first team at Central Park, he would go on to score 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan, and tales of his feats would be passed down through generations. There are very few down at the Brick Community Stadium these days who don't know of Sir Billy, young or old, his name carried a cache right until his last.Great Britain gave him the international recognition denied to him by Wales, and he rewarded the selectors by racking up the tries, particularly against the Australians who would bear the brunt of his scoring ability.He scored 36 tries alone on his maiden Great Britain tour, dazzling both Australia and New Zealand in 1954 under captain and fellow Welshman Dickie Williams.Boston was a phenomenal rugby league player, but there is also a powerful message in how in post-war Britain a black athlete could become a hugely popular figure by communities adjusting to a new, more diverse world.Others like Roy Francis beforehand, Johnny Freeman, and Colin Dixon, also became established names, but never quite sprinkled the same stardust as Sir Billy.It paved the way for players such as Ellery Hanley and Martin Offiah to charm the public with their talents, while modern day talent such as Junior Nsemba and Kai Pearce-Paul continues to stand out in a sport which has broken down barriers for years.Sir Billy had a unique unifying effect on a normally partisan and tribal rugby league community. He was revered naturally in Wigan, his adopted home, but you won't hear a boo or jeer at mention of Boston anywhere - not even at sworn rivals St Helens where they appreciate a good footballer when they see one.Still a regular visitor to Wigan games right up to his passing, it was always a beautiful moment when the cameras found him, the crowd spotting him on the screen bursting into cheer, and the realisation creeping over his face in the shape of a smile.There was a photo of him and his wife Lady Joan, who had died just a few weeks previously, on her seat with flowers at Wigan's game with Wakefield last week. There is a poignancy that Sir Billy departed soon after her.His seat will always be reserved at Wigan, and he will be dearly missed but certainly not forgotten.

schema.headline: Sir Billy Boston: 'A world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told'

title: Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50%
description: Canada has announced counter-tariffs as high as 50% on a range of US goods in retaliation to the latest wave of levies on Canadian imports imposed by
body: Canada has announced counter-tariffs as high as 50% on a range of US goods in retaliation to the latest wave of levies on Canadian imports imposed by President Donald Trump last weekend. The Canadian tariffs will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) worth of American products, ranging from steel to furniture, fresh tuna and cotton T-shirts, officials announced on Tuesday.The list of targeted products is designed to match Canadian goods hit by the US. The Canadian levies are set to come into effect on 8 September.It is the latest escalation after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making last-minute demands that were unreasonable.Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said that Canada's retaliation is in response to 50% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on a range of Canadian goods after trade talks fell apart on Friday."Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses and communities across our nation," he said. "Canada must respond."Champagne characterised Canada's retaliation as "proportionate" and "strategic".He added that Canada will also offer businesses and workers impacted by US tariffs an additional C$7.5bn for support programmes designed to minimise job losses and keep companies afloat.Placing taxes on trade between what are historically two of the world's closest trading partners will undoubtedly lead to pain on both sides of the border.Supply chains which have been developed over decades are set to see increased trading costs due the latest tariff announcements made from both the US and Canada, ultimately hitting businesses of all sizes and consumers through potentially higher prices.Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support their government in holding firm against the US. But some questions remain on exactly why trade talks fell apart, with the Conservative opposition asking that the full text of the draft deal with the US be released. Businesses have also expressed concerns about the impact of a prolonged trade war with Canada's largest trading partner.The White House released a statement after Canada announced its counter-tariffs, saying that the US was prepared to offer Canada "the most preferential market access of any country on Earth" in recent trade talks."Instead of partnership, Canada chose unreasonable demands, walk-backs, and flat-out rejection," it said.In a series of Tuesday posts on Truth Social, Trump also accused Canada of "ripping off" the US for decades and of charging American farmers steep tariffs. "I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable," Trump wrote. "They feel entitled, but they are not a State, and will be entitled no longer!"He suggested that he will change the name of Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes on the US-Canada border, to Lake America, writing: "We don't expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer."Trump threatened this week to hike US tariffs on Canadian automobiles to 50% as of 1 January. Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by accusing Trump of wanting to "destroy" Canadian industries including the automobile manufacturing and steel and aluminum sectors. Public rhetoric on both sides reached a fever pitch on Monday, but some officials struck a more diplomatic tone on Tuesday with hopes that talks could be resumed.After calling Trump a "loser" on Monday at a news conference, Ontario Premier Doug Ford acknowledged in an interview with CNN that "things got a little heated"."But I want to make a deal — a good deal for the American people, a good deal for Canadians," Ford said.The escalation also puts into question the future of a North American free trade pact between Canada, the US and Mexico called the USMCA. President Claudia Sheinbaum had despatched her economy secretary, Marcelo Ebrard, to Washington for emergency talks after trade negotiations collapsed with Canada.

schema.headline: Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50%
